Photo by Markus Spiske on UnsplashRecently I took part in a Kaggle Playground competition, Predicting Stellar Class, and used it to test how far agentic coding tools like Claude Code, Codex, and a single folder of access have come for tabular Kaggle work. I came in 26th, and what stood out wasn’t the placement so much as how quickly a solid baseline came together. Generating a baseline notebook and submitting it from the terminal has become genuinely easy. I use Claude Code personally, but everything below applies just as well to any agentic coding tool or prompt window.
NVIDIA’s Trick to Acing Kaggle Competitions
Chris Deotte, a Kaggle Grandmaster at NVIDIA, recently ran the same playbook on a different Playground competition, Predicting Customer Churn. After it ended, he wrote up his approach to using agentic coding tools to generate and compete in Kaggle competitions. You can read the full writeup here: Winning a Kaggle Competition With Generative AI Assisted Coding. It walks through how he set up and performed well in these playground style competitions, and a lot of what follows is me applying and adapting the same ideas.
Using AI Tools for EDA
Before starting any analysis, I open a fresh Claude Code session with access to a new, dedicated folder. I personally prefer running the app in Auto mode from the start. Once the session has access, I share the train and test datasets along with all the competition details, then start from one of two prompts.
The first option is to ask Claude Code to read whatever public baseline is already shared on Kaggle and suggest ways to experiment on top of it:
read the shared public baseline from Kaggle and give some ideas to experiment with this baselineThis tends to explain the baseline well and points to tools worth using, but I have found the suggestions here can be a bit generic and overly parametric.
The second option, and the one Chris recommends as the ideal starting point, is to skip the public baseline entirely and start from the raw data:
Please write and run EDA code to understand the CSV files train.csv and test.csvUsing Agents for Building Baselines
For turning that EDA into an actual model, Chris suggests a straightforward pipeline prompt:
"Please write full code pipeline to read train.csv and test.csv and train a
kfold XGBoost model. Save the OOF (out of fold predictions) and the Test PREDS
to disk as Numpy files. Display the metric score each fold and overall."The one thing I always add on top of this is a rule for Claude Code to treat cross validation as the ground truth for Playground competitions. When comparing different baselines, whether that’s a neural net against a GBDT or two feature sets against each other, CV is always the metric the decision gets made on.
Designing Feature Engineering Experiments
There is no single fixed way to approach this stage. Once I have a baseline CV score, I run experiments inspired by competition discussions, public notebooks from other entrants, and occasionally ideas pulled straight from research papers, and I build each one out with Claude Code. Running these iteratively and keeping every idea that actually improves the model is what compounds into a genuinely strong model over time. For every experiment, good or bad, I save the OOF and test predictions to disk.
This next part is Chris Deotte’s framing directly: to generate new ideas, we can either propose them ourselves or have LLMs generate them. There are several effective ways to prompt LLMs into producing good ideas here:

• Ask LLMs to find and read research papers on the topic.

• Ask LLMs to read forums and publicly shared code on the topic.

• Have LLMs perform EDA to determine relationships between features and targets for feature engineering.

• Ask LLMs for ideas based on the current knowledge base.

• Have humans brainstorm with LLMs and create ideas together.
Ensemble Models & Saving Results in Tabular Form
Once distillation and idea combination produce a new round of experiments, I’m left with hundreds of OOF and test prediction files, each one a candidate for the final blend. Rather than eyeballing which pair looks complementary, I hand this to the agent as a search problem: combine all the OOF/test PREDs using several meta models, hill climbing, ridge regression, logistic regression, and report back on OOF CV score, not training fit.
Hill climbing is my default starting point, and it’s a technique I picked up from Chris Deotte, who has written extensively on Kaggle about using it to build strong ensembles from large pools of OOF predictions. It’s greedy but effective at this scale: start from the single best model, iterate through the full pool of predictions, add whichever one improves the OOF blend the most, repeat until nothing helps anymore. Ridge and logistic regression give a different lens: they solve for optimal linear weights across all models simultaneously, which sometimes surfaces combinations hill climbing’s greedy path misses, especially when several models are highly correlated with each other.
This step takes real time, trying every meta model against every subset of hundreds of prediction files isn’t a quick loop. I generally kick this off in Auto mode and let the agent run through the combinations on its own rather than babysitting each attempt, checking back once it has results rather than approving every step. I also have it log every combination it tries into a single tabular results file: model names/IDs, blend weights, meta model used, OOF score, and leaderboard score once submitted. That table becomes the real artifact I keep coming back to, the source of truth for what’s been tried and what worked, turning a folder of hundreds of loose prediction files into something I can sort and reason about in seconds.
Takeaway
None of this replaces understanding the problem. What it replaces is the hours spent typing out boilerplate: kfold loops, EDA scaffolding, ensemble search code. Handing that off to an agent, with CV kept as the one metric that actually decides anything, is what let a 26th place Playground result come out of a few focused sessions instead of a few focused days. Chris Deotte’s writeup is worth reading in full if you want the source rather than my adaptation of it. 1st Place Solution WriteUp “Predicting Customer Churn”
